title: Clam Bake in a Pot
subtitle: one-pot seafood feast with corn and sausage
excerpt: A traditional New England clam bake made in a single large pot on the hob. Clams, prawns, sausage, corn, and potatoes all cook together in a seasoned broth. Serve straight from the pot with butter and lemon.
sourceNotes: The New England clam bake is a coastal tradition going back to Native American cooking methods. Traditionally done on the beach with seaweed, it is now more often made on the hob.

content.text: Layer the ingredients in the right order -- potatoes and sausage go in first as they take longest. Seafood goes in last. Everything cooks in the same fragrant broth and absorbs the flavours around it.

items.prepNote: use 500g clams -- add 300g raw prawns in the last 5 minutes
use smoked sausage or kielbasa, cut into chunks
use 2 corn cobs, cut into chunks

content.text: Fill a very large pot with 2 litres of water. Add the salt, bay leaves, and thyme. Bring to a boil.
Add the potatoes and sausage. Cook for 15 minutes.
Add the corn cobs. Cook for 5 more minutes.
Add the clams. Cover and cook for 5 minutes until they open. Discard any that stay closed.
Add the prawns. Cook for 3 to 5 minutes until pink and cooked through.
Use a ladle to divide everything between large bowls or serve from the pot. Pour over some of the broth.
Add a knob of butter to each bowl and serve with lemon wedges.

items.cause: Dead clams or not cooked long enough
items.fix: Discard any clams that remain closed after 8 minutes. They are not safe to eat.

items.symptom: Potatoes are still hard when seafood is done
items.cause: Potatoes cut too large or not given enough time
items.fix: Cut potatoes into smaller pieces next time. Parboil them for 5 extra minutes at the start.

items.cause: Not enough seasoning in the water
items.fix: The broth should be well salted like pasta water. Add salt generously at the start.

content.text: The New England clam bake traces its origins to the Indigenous peoples of the northeast coast, who cooked seafood in pits lined with heated rocks and covered with seaweed. European settlers adopted and adapted the tradition. Today it is a summer celebration food along the coast of Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut. The pot version brings the same festive spirit to any kitchen.
